questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 7 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. Why is 4 red impossible?
questions.explanation: The success count is bounded by available red tokens.

questions.stem: The success proportion is 0.35. What is the failure proportion?
questions.explanation: Binary outcome proportions add to 1.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD when constructing an interval for the mean.
choices: A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.
A prediction interval for a single future observation.
A proportion interval regardless of variable type.

questions.stem: The 95th percentile of a sample-mean distribution is 14. What does it describe?
questions.explanation: The percentile belongs to the sampling distribution, not automatically the individual distribution.
choices: 95% of all individuals must be at most 14.
About 95% of repeated sample means are at most 14.

questions.stem: A systematic sample starts at ID 3 and takes every tenth ID. Which IDs appear first?
questions.explanation: Add ten to the starting ID at each selection.

questions.stem: A normal model has mean 50 and SD 2. Which interval contains about 99.7%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses three SD on each side.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 10. One new observation equal to 10 is added. What happens to the mean?
questions.explanation: Adding a value equal to the current mean preserves that mean.

questions.stem: X is uniform from 2 to 10. What can be said about P(X>12)?
questions.explanation: The event lies entirely outside the model's support.
choices: It is the density height at 12.

questions.stem: An inspector checks a fixed batch of independent items with the same defect chance. Which variable fits a binomial model?
questions.explanation: A binomial variable counts occurrences in a fixed number of trials.
choices: The exact mass of the first item.
The attempt on which the first defect is found.
The number of defective items found.
The average time needed to check an item.

questions.stem: For two trials with positive chance of two failures, how do exactly one failure and at least one failure compare?
questions.explanation: At least one includes both exactly one and two failures.
choices: At least one has greater probability.

questions.stem: A sample is drawn without replacement from a box containing marked and unmarked cards. When must the sample contain a marked card?
questions.explanation: There are too few unmarked cards to fill a sample larger than their number.
choices: Only if every card in the box is marked.
When the sample size exceeds the number of unmarked cards.
Whenever one marked card is present in the box.
Whenever the sample size is less than the number of unmarked cards.

questions.stem: A question asks for the mass exceeded by only 10% of packages. What units should the answer have?
questions.explanation: The requested answer is an original-scale cutoff, not a probability.
choices: No units because it is a z-score automatically.

questions.stem: Daily print totals are shown in a histogram instead of a time-series graph. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: A histogram summarizes the distribution without retaining chronology.
choices: Which total occurred on which date.

questions.stem: Two distinct terminal paths describe exactly one head in two tosses. How is their combined probability found?
questions.explanation: Distinct terminal outcomes are disjoint, so their probabilities add.
choices: Subtract the smaller from the larger.
Ignore one because both describe one head.

questions.stem: Two services have mean wait 10 minutes, but SDs 1 and 6 minutes. What does the larger SD suggest?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation describes variation around a center, not an extra amount added to it.
choices: The mean must actually be 16 minutes.
Every wait is six minutes longer.
Waits vary more around the same mean.

questions.stem: A supplied sampling model gives P(mean<=12)=0.90. What is P(mean>12)?
questions.explanation: The two events are complements.

questions.stem: Which question targets a population proportion?
questions.explanation: A proportion summarizes membership in a defined yes/no outcome.
choices: What fraction of jobs finish on time?
What is the mean duration of jobs?
What is the SD of file sizes?
What is the median number of pages?

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: For a continuous duration, how do P(X<6) and P(X<=6) compare?
questions.explanation: An individual boundary point has zero probability.
choices: The second is always twice the first.
They differ by the density height at 6.

questions.stem: X counts trials through first success. What does X>3 require?
questions.explanation: Waiting more than three trials means no success in those trials.
choices: Failures on the first three trials.
At least one success in the first three trials.

questions.stem: The plus-four estimate adds two successes and two failures. With 8 successes out of 40, what adjusted fraction is used?
questions.explanation: The adjusted count is x+2 and the adjusted total is n+4.

questions.stem: Two mixed populations have the same size, but one has a larger share of faulty cables. Both are sampled randomly without replacement at the same sample size. How do their expected faulty counts compare?
questions.explanation: The population with the larger faulty share yields more faulty cables on average.
choices: The expected counts depend only on whether order is recorded.
The expected count is higher for the population with a larger faulty share.
The expected count is lower for the population with a larger faulty share.
The expected counts are equal because the sample sizes agree.

questions.stem: Half of tablet users use laptops, and half of non-tablet users use laptops. What does this suggest in these data?
questions.explanation: Equal conditional rates across the groups support independence in the empirical table.
choices: Every student uses exactly one device.
Laptop use does not depend on tablet-use status.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: They have equal means, but the second has more spread.
The second has a larger mean.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Which report matches its target?
questions.explanation: The reported target is the population mean, with confidence understood as procedure coverage.
choices: The median is guaranteed to equal 12.
The procedure estimates the population mean duration between 10 and 14 minutes.
Every future duration will be between 10 and 14.
Exactly 95 of the next 100 durations will lie there.

questions.stem: Independent sample size quadruples with population SD fixed. What happens to SE of the mean?
questions.explanation: SE scales as 1/sqrt(n), so a fourfold n reduces it by a factor of two.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A density is flat at height 2 over a half-unit interval and zero elsewhere. Is height 2 alone a problem?
questions.explanation: A density can exceed 1; probabilities are areas, and the full area here is 2 times 0.5.
choices: No; total area may be any positive number.
Yes; every density height must be at most 1.
No; its total area is 1, and height is not probability.

figure.alt: A rectangular density has height 2 from 0 to 0.5 and is zero outside.

data.alt: A rectangular density has height 2 from 0 to 0.5 and is zero outside.

questions.stem: A timer reports durations to the nearest second. What follows about the underlying duration?
questions.explanation: Recording precision does not make the underlying measurement discrete.
choices: It may vary continuously despite rounded records.
It cannot be less than one second.
It must change only in whole seconds.

questions.stem: A strongly skewed variable is converted to z-scores. Does it become normal?
questions.explanation: A linear transformation preserves distributional shape.
choices: No; standardization shifts and rescales without removing skew.
Yes; every z-score distribution is standard normal.
Yes; subtracting the mean removes the tail.

questions.stem: One student counts failed attempts before the first success. Another counts all attempts through the first success. How are their variables related?
questions.explanation: The two variables describe the same sequence with different counting conventions.
choices: Neither count can be known when the first success occurs.
The first includes one extra trial.
The second includes one extra trial, the success itself.

questions.stem: A report gives 30 successes among 120 observations. Which is the estimate of population success proportion?
questions.explanation: The success count must be divided by the total to estimate the proportion.

questions.stem: A count variable has expected value 0.4. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: An expectation is an average, not necessarily a possible individual value.
choices: Its long-run average can be 0.4 despite integer observations.
A single session must contain 0.4 events.
Exactly 40% of sessions must contain one event.

questions.stem: Given that a U(0,12) wait exceeds 4, what shape describes the total wait's conditional density?
questions.explanation: Restricting a uniform density to a subinterval and renormalizing preserves flatness there.

questions.stem: The ordered data are 2, 4, 4, 7, 20. What is the median?
questions.explanation: The middle observation is the third value, 4.

questions.stem: Two normal curves share SD but have different means. What is equal?
questions.explanation: A common SD gives identical shape and width; different means shift the curves.
choices: Their probabilities below every fixed cutoff.

questions.stem: The number of independent items rises from 25 to 100. What happens to expected sum and SD of sum?
questions.explanation: Sum mean scales with n and sum SD with sqrt(n).
choices: Expected sum stays fixed; SD halves.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval estimates a population use rate. Does 95% mean that 95% of the population uses the service?
questions.explanation: Confidence level and the estimated parameter are different quantities.
choices: No; it means 95 people were surveyed.
Yes; confidence equals the use rate.
No; 95% describes the interval procedure's coverage.

questions.stem: Why report a confidence interval instead of only a sample mean?
questions.explanation: An interval communicates estimation precision beyond a single point estimate.
choices: It guarantees the true mean is the midpoint.
It expresses uncertainty in estimating the population mean.

questions.stem: A first branch has probability 0.4; its next conditional branch is 0.5. What is the path probability?
questions.explanation: Multiply probabilities along a path.

questions.stem: Which wording is most neutral for a parking survey?
questions.explanation: Neutral wording avoids suggesting the desired evaluation.
choices: Do you support the unfair parking fee?
Do you oppose the helpful parking fee?
Do you support the proposed parking fee?
Why do you dislike the parking fee?

questions.stem: The sample is an unordered set of cables. Why count combinations rather than different orders of the same set?
questions.explanation: Unordered sampling treats permutations of the same selected set as one sample.
choices: Reordering the same selected cables does not create a new sample set.
Selection order determines whether a cable is faulty.
Every sample set has only one cable.

questions.stem: X is uniform from 2 to 10. To find P(0<X<5), which portion contributes area?
questions.explanation: There is no density outside the support, so only the overlap contributes.

questions.stem: Notebook colors are blue, blue, black, red. Which statement meaningfully summarizes a typical category?
questions.explanation: A most-common category is meaningful without arbitrary arithmetic on labels.
choices: The standard deviation of color names is 1.
Blue is the most common color.

questions.stem: A fixed-size sample is randomly selected from a batch of known good and faulty bulbs. Each selected bulb is set aside. Which model fits the number of good bulbs selected?
questions.explanation: The procedure counts one category in a fixed-size sample from a finite population without replacement.

questions.stem: A small random independent sample comes from a normal population. Is n<30 alone a reason to reject a t interval?
questions.explanation: Conditions matter; small n is not an automatic disqualification for normal data.
choices: Yes; t requires at least 30 in every case.
No; it must use a proportion interval.
No; small normal samples can support the t method.

questions.stem: Individual masses have SD 20 g; means of 25 independent masses have SD 4 g. Which spread applies to one package?
questions.explanation: The individual distribution keeps its own SD; the mean uses a smaller SE.

questions.stem: Which event is the complement of at least one failure in three trials?
questions.explanation: The only way to avoid any failure is to have none.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 8. One observation below 8 is removed. What happens to the mean of the remaining values?
questions.explanation: Removing a below-average observation raises the remaining average.

questions.stem: A normal model's mean increases, with SD fixed. At a fixed deadline, what happens to the probability of finishing before it?
questions.explanation: Shifting durations right moves area away from the fixed lower-tail deadline.

questions.stem: A bar graph of counts 98 and 100 starts its vertical axis at 97. What impression might it exaggerate?
questions.explanation: A truncated baseline can make a small count difference appear visually large.
choices: The size of the difference between the counts.

questions.stem: All values and their mean and SD are converted from meters to centimeters. What happens to z-scores?
questions.explanation: The conversion factor cancels in the standardized ratio.

questions.stem: Students choosing tutoring score higher. Why is a causal claim uncertain?
questions.explanation: A self-selected comparison can mix tutoring effects with other differences.
choices: Motivation may affect both tutoring attendance and scores.
Any score difference proves a tutoring effect.
A larger score difference removes all confounding.

questions.stem: X counts broken cables in independent checks. Can broken be called success in a binomial model?
questions.explanation: Success is a modeling label, not a value judgment.
choices: Only if no cables are broken.
Only if more than half are broken.
Yes; success means the counted outcome.

questions.stem: The success chance improves after each failed attempt because the process learns. Why is a geometric model questionable?
questions.explanation: Geometric waiting assumes independent trials with a constant success chance.
choices: The success probability is not constant.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Someone says n=30 guarantees normal sample means for every population. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: There is no universal cutoff guaranteeing a good normal approximation.
choices: Thirty is too large for any sample.
Skewness and extreme observations affect how large n needs to be.
Sample means can never approach normality.
Only populations with mean zero qualify.

questions.stem: A service meets its deadline with probability 0.80. What is the probability of missing it?
questions.explanation: The complement has probability 1-0.80.

questions.stem: A rate is stated per hour but a cutoff is inserted as a number of minutes. What must be done before using the tail formula?
questions.explanation: The rate-time product must use matching units.
choices: Round the probability to an integer.
Express rate and cutoff in compatible time units.
Multiply both numbers by the sample size.
Replace the cutoff with the mean.

questions.stem: For a comparison holding the observed proportion and confidence fixed, n quadruples. What happens to estimated margin?
questions.explanation: The estimated SE and margin scale with 1/sqrt(n).

questions.stem: A basic box plot reports minimum 0, Q1=2, median 3, Q3=4, maximum 20. Which comparison is supported?
questions.explanation: Using the displayed summary, the upper segment spans 20-4=16 units and the lower segment spans 2-0=2 units. Segment length describes numerical spread, not an exact observation count; quartile conventions and ties can affect those counts.
choices: The segment from Q3 to the maximum spans a wider numerical range than the segment from the minimum to Q1.
The upper segment must contain three times as many observations.
The lower segment contains no observations.
The plot establishes the exact mean.

figure.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

data.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

questions.stem: A fitted normal model predicts 2% above a cutoff, while a large observed dataset has 18% above it. What should be investigated?
questions.explanation: A large model-data discrepancy warrants checking fit and assumptions.
choices: Whether observations should be changed to fit the model.
Only the number of decimal places.
Whether the model fits the observed tail.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Which report matches its target?
questions.explanation: The reported target is the population mean, with confidence understood as procedure coverage.
choices: Every future duration will be between 10 and 14.
The procedure estimates the population mean duration between 10 and 14 minutes.
Exactly 95 of the next 100 durations will lie there.
The median is guaranteed to equal 12.

questions.stem: Normal models have the same mean. For a fixed cutoff below that mean, which has the larger lower-tail probability?
questions.explanation: A wider curve places more area beyond a fixed cutoff away from its center.
choices: The model with the larger SD.
The one with more recorded observations regardless of SD.
The model with the smaller SD.

questions.stem: Sample mean is 12 and margin of error is 2. What interval results?
questions.explanation: Add and subtract the margin from the estimate.

figure.alt: Interval from 10 to 14 with its center marked at 12.

data.alt: Interval from 10 to 14 with its center marked at 12.

questions.stem: A score is reported at approximately the 90th percentile. What kind of information does that give?
questions.explanation: A percentile describes relative position, not percentage correct. This question does not require an exact rank, tie rule, or interpolation convention.
choices: That 90% of exam answers were correct.
Its position relative to other scores.

questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 7 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. Why is 4 red impossible?
questions.explanation: The success count is bounded by available red tokens.

questions.stem: Students rate a service while its manager watches. Compared with anonymous responses, what might happen?
questions.explanation: Pressure or perceived consequences can influence responses.

questions.stem: Which quantity naturally has discrete possible values?
questions.explanation: Counts take separated integer values, unlike continuous measurements.
choices: The exact mass of a package.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: An exact continuous duration has P(X=4)=0. Can a timer report 4 seconds?
questions.explanation: A rounded recorded value can have positive probability even though an exact point has zero area.
choices: Only if the density equals zero everywhere.
No; 4 seconds can never be recorded.
Only if the model becomes discrete before rounding.
Yes; rounding collects a positive-width interval of exact values.

questions.stem: Score A is 10 above its mean with SD 5; score B is 12 above its mean with SD 12. Which is relatively farther above its group mean?
questions.explanation: A is 2 SD above its mean; B is 1 SD above.
choices: The larger raw score difference always wins.

questions.stem: Two samples have the same observed mean above a claimed population mean and the same population SD, but sizes 25 and 100. Which mean is farther above in SE units?
questions.explanation: The larger sample has smaller SE, making the same absolute gap more SE units.
choices: The larger sample changes the claimed mean.

questions.stem: A symmetric central normal interval contains 90%. How much area lies in each outside tail?
questions.explanation: The excluded 10% splits equally between the tails.

questions.stem: A probability table totals 1 but contains one entry of -0.1. What follows?
questions.explanation: Both nonnegativity and total 1 are required.
choices: It is valid if the mean is positive.
Negative probabilities simply indicate rare events.
It is valid because only the total matters.
It is invalid because probabilities cannot be negative.

questions.stem: A well-run randomized experiment finds better results for an app among its volunteers. Which claim needs extra caution?
questions.explanation: Generalization depends on the volunteers and setting, beyond random assignment.
choices: The same effect applies to all students everywhere.
Random assignment helped compare the formats.
The observed volunteers had different average results.
The study provides evidence about an app effect in this setting.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50. Where are unbiased random-sample means centered?
questions.explanation: The expected sample mean equals the population mean under the sampling assumptions.

questions.stem: Two reasonable quartile methods give upper outlier fences of 18 and 20 for the same dataset. One observation is 35. Which conclusion agrees with both methods?
questions.explanation: The value 35 is well above both reported fences, so choosing between these conventions does not change the flag. An outlier flag alone does not establish a recording error.
choices: The observation is not flagged under either method.
The observation must be a recording error.
Only the method with fence 18 flags the observation.
The observation is flagged as unusually high under both methods.

questions.stem: Why use planning proportion 0.5 when no prior estimate is available?
questions.explanation: The largest Bernoulli variance is at p=0.5, so planning protects against smaller assumed variation.
choices: It guarantees half the population has the trait.
It maximizes p(1-p), giving a conservative required sample size.
It makes the sample unbiased automatically.
It minimizes all margins to zero.

questions.stem: Two mixed populations have the same size, but one has a larger share of faulty cables. Both are sampled randomly without replacement at the same sample size. How do their expected faulty counts compare?
questions.explanation: The population with the larger faulty share yields more faulty cables on average.
choices: The expected count is higher for the population with a larger faulty share.
The expected counts are equal because the sample sizes agree.
The expected counts depend only on whether order is recorded.
The expected count is lower for the population with a larger faulty share.

questions.stem: A team redraws randomly from a mixed deck, replacing and remixing each card. It stops at the first heart. Which model describes the number of draws?
questions.explanation: Replacement supports a constant chance, and the stopping rule is the first success.

questions.stem: A question asks for the mass exceeded by only 10% of packages. What units should the answer have?
questions.explanation: The requested answer is an original-scale cutoff, not a probability.
choices: No units because it is a z-score automatically.

questions.stem: A known-SD mean interval currently has margin 1. To target margin 0.5 at the same confidence, how should n change?
questions.explanation: Halving a square-root-based margin requires four times the observations.

questions.stem: A wait is uniform from 0 to 12 minutes. What is P(3<X<6)?
questions.explanation: The interval occupies 3 of the support's 12 minutes.

questions.stem: A student treats z=2 as a probability of 2. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Z-scores can exceed 1, while probabilities cannot.
choices: A normal model cannot have positive z-scores.
A z-score must be a percentage.
A standardized distance is not an area probability.

questions.stem: What puts an upper limit on the number of marked cards in a sample drawn without replacement?
questions.explanation: The sample cannot include more marked cards than it has slots or than the box contains.
choices: Both the sample size and the number of marked cards in the box.
Only the number of unmarked cards in the box.
Only the probability of a marked card on the first draw.

questions.stem: An exponential model has mean wait 4 minutes. What is its SD?
questions.explanation: For an exponential distribution, mean and SD are both the reciprocal of the rate.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Fifty readings taken seconds apart from one fluctuating machine are treated as independent. What should be checked?
questions.explanation: Correlation can undermine the usual independent-observation SE formula.
choices: Whether the mean can be calculated.

questions.stem: A sample has 8 observations. Its sum of squared deviations is already supplied. Which divisor gives sample variance?
questions.explanation: Sample variance uses n-1, unlike the population calculation with all population members.

questions.stem: Which change best addresses a poll that includes only frequent library users?
questions.explanation: Correcting coverage is more important than enlarging the same biased sample.
choices: Collect ten times as many frequent-user responses.

questions.stem: A sample variance is 9 minutes squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and returns to the original units.

questions.stem: A proportion estimate is 0.40 with margin 0.05. What interval is this in percentages?
questions.explanation: Convert the endpoints 0.35 and 0.45 to percentages.

questions.stem: Normal models have the same mean. For a fixed cutoff below that mean, which has the larger lower-tail probability?
questions.explanation: A wider curve places more area beyond a fixed cutoff away from its center.
choices: The model with the smaller SD.
The one with more recorded observations regardless of SD.
The model with the larger SD.

questions.stem: A first branch has probability 0.4; its next conditional branch is 0.5. What is the path probability?
questions.explanation: Multiply probabilities along a path.

questions.stem: A supplied probability table lists P(X=0),...,P(X=8). To find P(X<=2), which entries are needed?
questions.explanation: At most 2 is a cumulative event including all counts through 2.

questions.stem: Sample SD is 6 minutes and n=9; sqrt(9)=3. What estimated SE is used?
questions.explanation: Estimated SE is s/sqrt(n) and retains the measurement units.

questions.stem: To halve SE, how must an independent sample's size change?
questions.explanation: Squaring the desired precision factor gives the sample-size factor.
choices: Add 4 regardless of its current size.

questions.stem: An exponential model has mean wait 4 minutes. What is its SD?
questions.explanation: For an exponential distribution, mean and SD are both the reciprocal of the rate.

questions.stem: A table has positive frequency at exactly 2 jobs. How do counts for fewer than 2 and at most 2 compare?
questions.explanation: At most includes the observations equal to the cutoff.
choices: Fewer than 2 has the larger count.
Neither can be found from exact frequencies.
At most 2 has the larger count.

questions.stem: Among 200 recorded jobs, 30 were late. What does 30/200 describe?
questions.explanation: An empirical frequency summarizes observations and can estimate a probability.
choices: A guarantee that the next job is late.
The exact long-run probability under every possible condition.
The number of late jobs that must occur tomorrow.

questions.stem: For a standard normal variable, compare P(Z<-1.4) and P(Z>1.4).
questions.explanation: Normal symmetry makes opposite equal-distance tails equal.

questions.stem: Two reasonable quartile methods give upper outlier fences of 18 and 20 for the same dataset. One observation is 35. Which conclusion agrees with both methods?
questions.explanation: The value 35 is well above both reported fences, so choosing between these conventions does not change the flag. An outlier flag alone does not establish a recording error.
choices: Only the method with fence 18 flags the observation.
The observation is not flagged under either method.
The observation must be a recording error.
The observation is flagged as unusually high under both methods.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.

questions.stem: Only 5% exceed cutoff k. Which percentile is k?
questions.explanation: The remaining 95% lies at or below the cutoff.

questions.stem: Compare U(0,12) and U(20,32). What is true about their standard deviations?
questions.explanation: A common shift changes center without changing spread.
choices: The second is larger because its mean is larger.
The first is larger because it includes zero.

questions.stem: A symmetric confidence interval is 8 to 12. What point estimate is at its center?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the estimate, not either endpoint.

questions.stem: A game has negative expected net gain. Can a player still win money on one play?
questions.explanation: An average loss does not rule out individual wins.
choices: No; every outcome must lose money.
Only after the expected value changes.
Yes, if positive-gain outcomes have positive probability.
No; the largest prize must be negative.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, how does the mean compare with the median?
questions.explanation: The high value pulls the mean above the median of 3.
choices: No comparison is possible without a calculator.

questions.stem: What equation describes a continuous model's 90th percentile k?
questions.explanation: The percentile cutoff has the stated area to its left.

questions.stem: Datasets share min=0 and max=100, but have different IQRs. What follows?
questions.explanation: Range uses endpoints while IQR uses quartile positions.
choices: Equal ranges do not imply equal middle-half spread.
Their standard deviations must be identical.

questions.stem: A package is accepted if 490<mass<520. Which part of its normal curve should be shaded?
questions.explanation: A between-cutoffs event corresponds to the intervening area.

figure.alt: A normal density with vertical boundary lines at 490 and 520; no area is preselected.

data.alt: A normal density with vertical boundary lines at 490 and 520; no area is preselected.

questions.stem: A researcher deletes genuine results that disagree with the desired conclusion. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: Valid observations cannot be discarded merely because they are unfavorable.
choices: A smaller dataset guarantees less bias.
The report no longer fairly represents the collected evidence.
Any unusual observation is automatically an error.
Deleting inconvenient values always improves accuracy.

questions.stem: Tokens are replaced and mixed after each draw. Compared with leaving them out, what does replacement preserve?
questions.explanation: Replacement restores the composition before the next randomized draw.
choices: A decreasing total number of tokens.
The same token being selected every time.
The original color probabilities on each independent draw.

questions.stem: For n=20, a total exceeding 240 is equivalent to which mean event?
questions.explanation: Divide the total cutoff by the fixed sample size.

questions.stem: X has mean 50, SD 10. Which standard-normal event corresponds to X<60?
questions.explanation: Subtract the mean and divide by SD without reversing the inequality.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 8. One observation below 8 is removed. What happens to the mean of the remaining values?
questions.explanation: Removing a below-average observation raises the remaining average.

questions.stem: The numbers of pages in six jobs are 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 5. Which statement about the mode is correct?
questions.explanation: The values 2 and 4 each occur twice, more often than any other value.
choices: The mode is 3, halfway between 2 and 4.

questions.stem: For one normal model, P(X<40)=0.20 and P(X<60)=0.85. What is P(40<X<60)?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative lower-tail areas.

questions.stem: Students choosing tutoring score higher. Why is a causal claim uncertain?
questions.explanation: A self-selected comparison can mix tutoring effects with other differences.
choices: A larger score difference removes all confounding.
Any score difference proves a tutoring effect.
Motivation may affect both tutoring attendance and scores.

questions.stem: A model has one blank probability entry and lists every possible value. What does the blank need to account for?
questions.explanation: The outcomes in the completed table must account for the entire probability mass.
choices: The average of the listed probabilities.
All probability not already assigned to the other values.
Half the total probability, regardless of the other entries.
The probability of the most likely listed value.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: A sample of 200 is drawn without replacement from 500. Does it meet the course's at-most-10% independence guideline?
questions.explanation: The sample fraction is 200/500, well above 10%.
choices: Yes; every random sample meets the guideline.
No; it is 40% of the population.
No; samples must contain fewer than 10 observations.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: Durations are rounded to the nearest whole second. Ignoring tie conventions at boundaries, which exact interval reports as 4?
questions.explanation: Nearest-unit rounding collects values within half a unit of 4.

questions.stem: At fixed n and confidence, known population SD doubles. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Margin and full width are proportional to population SD.

questions.stem: A payout variable is measured in dollars. What units belong to its variance?
questions.explanation: Variance uses squared deviations from the expected payout.

questions.stem: Which question targets a population proportion?
questions.explanation: A proportion summarizes membership in a defined yes/no outcome.
choices: What is the SD of file sizes?
What is the mean duration of jobs?
What is the median number of pages?
What fraction of jobs finish on time?

questions.stem: A sample of 6 has strong skewness and an extreme outlier. What is sensible about a t interval?
questions.explanation: The small sample may not support the normality assumptions of the usual t method.
choices: It is automatically reliable because t has heavy tails.
The outlier must be removed without investigation.
Six observations guarantee a normal sampling distribution.

questions.stem: An event is described as drawing a heart or a king. Does the king of hearts qualify?
questions.explanation: Inclusive OR includes outcomes satisfying either or both conditions.
choices: Yes; the statistical OR includes the overlap.
Only if hearts and kings are independent.
Only if the card is drawn twice.

questions.stem: Four jobs have a mean of 5 pages. What is the total number of pages?
questions.explanation: Total equals number of observations times their mean.

questions.stem: Two binomial settings have the same fixed number of trials. One has a greater chance of success on each trial. What changes?
questions.explanation: A higher chance of success raises the average count while the trial count still bounds the result.
choices: The expected number of successes is greater in that setting.
Every run in that setting yields more successes.
The maximum possible number of successes is greater in that setting.
Both settings have the same expected number of successes.

questions.stem: About 99.7% lies within 3 SD in a normal model. About what percent lies outside on both sides combined?
questions.explanation: The combined outside area is 100%-99.7%.

questions.stem: A game charges a fixed entry fee and sometimes awards a prize. What distinguishes net gain from the prize amount?
questions.explanation: A player pays the fee whether or not a prize is awarded.
choices: Net gain accounts for the fee paid to play.
Net gain equals the largest possible prize.
Net gain ignores outcomes with no prize.
The fee changes the chance of each prize.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Independent observations come from an exactly normal population. Is n>=30 necessary for their mean to be normal?
questions.explanation: Independent normal observations have an exactly normal average.
choices: Yes; normal means are impossible below 30.
No; the mean instead becomes uniform.
Yes; individual normality disappears in small samples.
No; their mean is normal for any positive sample size.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A proposed density dips below zero over an interval. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Nonnegative density is required for nonnegative interval probabilities.
choices: Every valid density must be symmetric.
It would assign negative area to that interval.
A density must be flat everywhere.

questions.stem: Four mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories have reported proportions 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, and 0.25. What needs checking?
questions.explanation: Exhaustive nonoverlapping categories must have total probability or relative frequency 1.

questions.stem: Which model assigns equal probability to all equal-length subintervals within its support?
questions.explanation: Flat density, not continuity alone, gives equal interval areas.

questions.stem: A report gives 30 successes among 120 observations. Which is the estimate of population success proportion?
questions.explanation: The success count must be divided by the total to estimate the proportion.

questions.stem: Both endpoints of a uniform model increase by 4. What happens to its mean and SD?
questions.explanation: A translation shifts location but preserves distances.
choices: SD rises by 4; mean stays unchanged.
Mean rises by 4; SD stays unchanged.

questions.stem: A public dataset includes names beside individual survey answers. Which change best protects privacy while preserving group summaries?
questions.explanation: De-identification can preserve useful aggregate evidence while reducing identification risks.
choices: Replace every answer with the overall mean.
Keep names and omit the study methods.

questions.stem: On a die, A is even and B is greater than 3. Which results satisfy at least one condition?
questions.explanation: The union includes all outcomes in either event, counting overlaps once.

questions.stem: Which design permits an exact binomial count model with independent randomized draws?
questions.explanation: Replacement and remixing preserve the same independent success chance.
choices: Replacing and remixing each drawn token.
Drawing without replacement until the box is empty.
Drawing most of a small population without replacement.

questions.stem: Most waits are short, but a few extend far toward large values. What determines the skew direction?
questions.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the long tail.
choices: The side with the tallest bar alone.
The long tail toward large values.

questions.stem: Four jobs have a mean of 5 pages. What is the total number of pages?
questions.explanation: Total equals number of observations times their mean.

questions.stem: A normal model's mean rises by 3 with SD fixed. What happens to its 90th percentile?
questions.explanation: Every fixed percentile shifts with the mean when spread stays fixed.

questions.stem: A histogram is made from 500 means, each based on 20 observations. How many values are in that histogram?
questions.explanation: Each sample contributes one statistic, so there are 500 plotted means.

questions.stem: Students rate a service while its manager watches. Compared with anonymous responses, what might happen?
questions.explanation: Pressure or perceived consequences can influence responses.

questions.stem: The wait until the next request is modeled as exponential with rate 4 per hour. What is its mean in minutes?
questions.explanation: Mean wait is one quarter hour, or 15 minutes.

questions.stem: A sample variance is 9 minutes squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and returns to the original units.

questions.stem: Among 20 tablet users, 12 also use laptops. What is P(laptop given tablet) in this sample?
questions.explanation: Conditioning restricts the denominator to tablet users.

questions.stem: A binomial experiment has many trials, but successes are so rare that only a few are expected. Why might a normal approximation be poor?
questions.explanation: A good normal approximation needs sufficiently many expected successes and failures.
choices: The count is automatically symmetric because there are many trials.
The expected number of successes is too small.
The expected number of failures must also be small.

questions.stem: All values and their mean and SD are converted from meters to centimeters. What happens to z-scores?
questions.explanation: The conversion factor cancels in the standardized ratio.

questions.stem: A narrow interval uses only the fastest successful jobs to estimate the mean for all jobs. What is its main limitation?
questions.explanation: Precision cannot repair systematically excluded outcomes.
choices: Biased selection can make the interval misleading despite narrow width.
Adding decimal places removes selection bias.

questions.stem: Six tokens are drawn without replacement from a small mixed box. What challenges an exact binomial model?
questions.explanation: Without replacement from a small population violates the independent constant-p trial model.
choices: The number of draws is fixed.
Draws change the composition and are dependent.

questions.stem: 40 of 100 sampled jobs succeed. What is the sample success proportion?
questions.explanation: Divide the success count by the sample size.

questions.stem: X counts trials through first success. What does X>3 require?
questions.explanation: Waiting more than three trials means no success in those trials.
choices: At least one success in the first three trials.
Failures on the first three trials.

questions.stem: In many sessions, 20% have no failures. How might this inform a model?
questions.explanation: Relative frequencies can estimate a distribution without imposing a fixed order.
choices: Infer that every fifth session must have no failures.
Use 0.20 as an empirical estimate for P(X=0).

questions.stem: A sample has 2 successes and 98 failures. Does a large total alone justify the ordinary normal-approximation proportion interval?
questions.explanation: The success-failure check concerns both counts, not just total n.
choices: No; proportions cannot be estimated at all.
No; the observed success count is too sparse.

questions.stem: A uniform interval centered at 10 doubles its width while keeping center 10. What happens?
questions.explanation: Uniform mean depends on midpoint; SD is proportional to width.

questions.stem: One game always pays its expected payout. Another has the same expected payout but offers several possible payouts. How do they differ?
questions.explanation: A fixed payout has no variability; equal means do not imply equal spreads.
choices: Only the second game has positive spread.
Their spreads must match because their means match.
Only the first game has positive spread.
Both games must have zero spread.

figure.alt: Game A has payout 5 with probability 1; Game B has payouts 0 and 10 with probability 0.5 each.

data.alt: Game A has payout 5 with probability 1; Game B has payouts 0 and 10 with probability 0.5 each.

questions.stem: A bell-shaped distribution has mean 20 and SD 2. Approximately which interval contains 95%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses about two standard deviations on each side for a bell-shaped distribution.

questions.stem: Ten independent trials each have success probability 0.3. X counts successes. What makes a binomial model appropriate?
questions.explanation: Those experimental conditions define the binomial setting.
choices: The expected count is an integer.
Fixed trial count, two outcomes, independence, and constant success chance.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD when constructing an interval for the mean.
choices: A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.
A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A prediction interval for a single future observation.

questions.stem: Which area of the approximating normal curve represents exactly one specified integer count?
questions.explanation: Continuity correction assigns the mass of one integer to the interval of points closest to it.
choices: The area between the midpoints separating that integer from its two neighbors.
The entire area to the right of the count.
The whole area between the two neighboring integers.
The height of the curve at the count.

questions.stem: A package is accepted if 490<mass<520. Which part of its normal curve should be shaded?
questions.explanation: A between-cutoffs event corresponds to the intervening area.

figure.alt: A normal density with vertical boundary lines at 490 and 520; no area is preselected.

data.alt: A normal density with vertical boundary lines at 490 and 520; no area is preselected.

questions.stem: Exact wait times are replaced by short, medium, and long categories. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories retain rank information but lose exact numerical distances.
choices: The ordering of the three categories.
The exact differences between wait times.

questions.stem: Two distinct terminal paths describe exactly one head in two tosses. How is their combined probability found?
questions.explanation: Distinct terminal outcomes are disjoint, so their probabilities add.
choices: Ignore one because both describe one head.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD when constructing an interval for the mean.
choices: A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.
A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A prediction interval for a single future observation.

questions.stem: A random sample of 80 enrolled students reports 30% support for later hours. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.explanation: A sample result is evidence about a population, not an exact census result.
choices: Exactly 30% of all students support later hours.
Exactly 24 students in the entire college support later hours.
30% describes the sample and estimates population support.

questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 7 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. Why is 4 red impossible?
questions.explanation: The success count is bounded by available red tokens.

questions.stem: A report gives 30 successes among 120 observations. Which is the estimate of population success proportion?
questions.explanation: The success count must be divided by the total to estimate the proportion.

questions.stem: SE is 4 at n=25. What is SE at n=100, with the same population SD and independence?
questions.explanation: Quadrupling n halves SE.

questions.stem: A payout variable is measured in dollars. What units belong to its variance?
questions.explanation: Variance uses squared deviations from the expected payout.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A continuous model has F(9)=0.80. What percent exceeds 9?
questions.explanation: The upper tail complements the cumulative probability.

questions.stem: A proposed normal model gives substantial probability to negative durations. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: A normal approximation may be poor when impossible values receive meaningful probability.
choices: It assigns appreciable probability to impossible values.
Normal distributions cannot model any positive variable.

questions.stem: A sample variance is 9 minutes squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and returns to the original units.

questions.stem: Using the reported quartiles, group A has Q1=3, Q3=9; group B has Q1=10, Q3=14. Which has greater IQR?
questions.explanation: Use the reported quartiles: the IQRs are 9-3=6 and 14-10=4. No choice of quartile algorithm is required.
choices: The larger median must determine the IQR.

questions.stem: A teacher draws cards without replacement until the first marked card. Why is the draw number generally neither binomial nor geometric?
questions.explanation: The stopping rule rules out binomial counting, and the changing pool violates the geometric assumptions.
choices: A success has to be a desirable outcome.
Stopping at the first success always makes the count binomial.
The trial count is not fixed, and the chance can change between draws.

questions.stem: For a comparison holding the observed proportion and confidence fixed, n quadruples. What happens to estimated margin?
questions.explanation: The estimated SE and margin scale with 1/sqrt(n).

questions.stem: After a specific interval is computed, what is correct about its relation to a fixed population mean?
questions.explanation: Frequentist coverage refers to random intervals before observing the data.
choices: The endpoints must equal the smallest and largest observation.
The fixed mean changes to fit it with probability 95%.
It either contains that mean or does not; 95% describes the procedure.
The mean occupies 95% of the interval.

questions.stem: 40 students use laptops, 25 use tablets, and 10 use both. Why subtract 10 when counting either device?
questions.explanation: Subtracting one copy of the overlap counts each person once.
choices: Both-device users must be excluded entirely.
Subtraction is required because the sample is random.
Adding the first two counts includes the overlap twice.
The overlap does not use either device.

figure.alt: Venn regions: 30 laptop only, 10 both, 15 tablet only. The illustrated universe is the 55 users of either device.

data.alt: Venn regions: 30 laptop only, 10 both, 15 tablet only. The illustrated universe is the 55 users of either device.

questions.stem: Arrival rates sharply rise at lunchtime. What is questionable about a single exponential waiting model over the whole day?
questions.explanation: A single exponential waiting model of this kind assumes a stable arrival rate.
choices: A constant rate across the whole period.

questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 7 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. Why is 4 red impossible?
questions.explanation: The success count is bounded by available red tokens.

questions.stem: A college wants each academic program represented in a survey. Which plan best achieves that directly?
questions.explanation: Sampling within each program ensures representation from those groups.
choices: Invite only students who previously complained.
Randomly sample students within every program.
Select the first students entering one room.

questions.stem: A proposed normal model gives substantial probability to negative durations. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: A normal approximation may be poor when impossible values receive meaningful probability.
choices: It assigns appreciable probability to impossible values.
Normal distributions cannot model any positive variable.

questions.stem: A supplied normal distribution of sample means gives cumulative probabilities 0.15 at 8 and 0.85 at 12. What is the probability between 8 and 12?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative areas at the endpoints.

questions.stem: The SD of a normal model increases while the mean stays fixed. What happens to its peak?
questions.explanation: Spreading the same area over a wider curve lowers its peak.
choices: It becomes lower as the curve spreads out.

questions.stem: All ten observations equal 5, so their median is 5. Are exactly half strictly below the median?
questions.explanation: Ties mean a median need not have half the values strictly below it.
choices: No; none are strictly below it.
Yes; every median splits strict inequalities equally.
No; a median cannot exist with ties.

questions.stem: Both endpoints of a uniform model increase by 4. What happens to its mean and SD?
questions.explanation: A translation shifts location but preserves distances.
choices: SD rises by 4; mean stays unchanged.
Mean rises by 4; SD stays unchanged.

questions.stem: X counts the successes. Which values satisfy fewer than 3 successes?
questions.explanation: Fewer than is a strict inequality and excludes 3.

questions.stem: The 95th percentile of a sample-mean distribution is 14. What does it describe?
questions.explanation: The percentile belongs to the sampling distribution, not automatically the individual distribution.
choices: About 95% of repeated sample means are at most 14.
95% of all individuals must be at most 14.

questions.stem: Using the same sample and method, confidence rises from 90% to 99%. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Higher coverage requires a larger critical multiplier and a wider interval.

questions.stem: One student counts failed attempts before the first success. Another counts all attempts through the first success. How are their variables related?
questions.explanation: The two variables describe the same sequence with different counting conventions.
choices: The first includes one extra trial.
The second includes one extra trial, the success itself.
Neither count can be known when the first success occurs.

questions.stem: A probability interval is widened to include its original interval plus a region of positive density. What happens to its probability?
questions.explanation: Adding positive area raises probability while the total remains at most 1.

questions.stem: A bar graph of counts 98 and 100 starts its vertical axis at 97. What impression might it exaggerate?
questions.explanation: A truncated baseline can make a small count difference appear visually large.
choices: The size of the difference between the counts.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, how does the mean compare with the median?
questions.explanation: The high value pulls the mean above the median of 3.
choices: No comparison is possible without a calculator.

questions.stem: Population SD is 12 and n=36, with independent observations. sqrt(36)=6. What is the mean's SE?
questions.explanation: Divide population SD by the supplied square root of sample size.

questions.stem: The sample is an unordered set of cables. Why count combinations rather than different orders of the same set?
questions.explanation: Unordered sampling treats permutations of the same selected set as one sample.
choices: Every sample set has only one cable.
Reordering the same selected cables does not create a new sample set.
Selection order determines whether a cable is faulty.

questions.stem: The success proportion is 0.35. What is the failure proportion?
questions.explanation: Binary outcome proportions add to 1.

questions.stem: All values and their mean and SD are converted from meters to centimeters. What happens to z-scores?
questions.explanation: The conversion factor cancels in the standardized ratio.

questions.stem: Which event is the complement of at least one failure in three trials?
questions.explanation: The only way to avoid any failure is to have none.

questions.stem: X is uniform from 0 to 12. Which symmetric interval contains the middle 50%?
questions.explanation: The middle half has half the full width and is centered at 6.

questions.stem: A box plot has median 6. Can it reveal exactly how many observations equal 5?
questions.explanation: A box plot compresses the data into a few summary positions.
choices: No; the summary does not retain those exact counts.

questions.stem: A sample-size formula returns 62.2 observations. Which planned integer size meets that minimum?
questions.explanation: Round a required minimum up to avoid falling short.

questions.stem: A college wants each academic program represented in a survey. Which plan best achieves that directly?
questions.explanation: Sampling within each program ensures representation from those groups.
choices: Randomly sample students within every program.
Invite only students who previously complained.
Select the first students entering one room.

questions.stem: A game charges a fixed entry fee and sometimes awards a prize. What distinguishes net gain from the prize amount?
questions.explanation: A player pays the fee whether or not a prize is awarded.
choices: Net gain equals the largest possible prize.
Net gain accounts for the fee paid to play.
Net gain ignores outcomes with no prize.
The fee changes the chance of each prize.
